solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Polish ambassador mostly utilised dispatch boxes

indicators.note: most of the word, so the last letter goes
encloses, as a box holds its contents

parts.note: SENT (utilised dispatch) without its last letter
HE = His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: A Polish envoy's diplomatic bag is being sent off, boxes and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital looks like the nationality, but it is the lustre. 'Utilised dispatch' is past-tense sending, SENT, docked by 'mostly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with Polish as the noun: the gloss left on a buffed surface, not the nationality.

clue.text: I got a dozen fish snapping and caught two of them?

definitions.text: I got a dozen fish snapping and caught two of them?

indicators.note: breaking, so the letters are shattered into a new order

explanation.surface: An angler boasts of landing twelve fish, a couple of them biting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: there are a dozen signs, and Pisces is two fish, so catching 'two of them' catches a sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisces, the fishes, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, pictured as two fish.

clue.text: Opening of exhibition in Paris one limits to Corot and Degas?

indicators.note: a word's opening is where it starts, so its first letter
the two boundary letters, first and last

parts.note: je = I in French, and I is one

indicators.note: what the word would be if spoken in Paris, so the French translation

parts.note: first and last letters of COROT

explanation.surface: A Paris exhibition opens with works by Corot and Degas, two French painters.
explanation.walkthrough: Degas is the painter in the surface, but split it as de-gas, to put gas out. 'One' is the pronoun I, which in French is JE.
explanation.definitionFit: To de-gas something is to eject gas from it, hence the question mark.

clue.text: City with no affluent quarters

indicators.note: to quarter troops is to lodge them in houses, so the outer word takes the letter in

explanation.surface: A city that has no wealthy districts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' looks like city districts but is a verb, to house. Norwich is a cathedral city in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Norwich is a city, the county town of Norfolk.

clue.text: One's returned reptile with it?

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters run the other way

explanation.surface: Someone's pet lizard has been brought back, and it has something with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a cryptic definition: an animal carrying a microchip is one that can be returned to its owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A microchip under the skin identifies a lost pet so it can be returned.

clue.text: Fur-clad creature's first in line for New Jersey production

indicators.note: what comes first in a word is its opening letter

parts.note: a mink, prized for its fur

indicators.note: as in 'swap X for Y', one letter stands in place of the other

parts.note: L, first of LINE, replaces N (new)

explanation.surface: A fur-coated animal leads the queue for a show in New Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: New Jersey is the American state in the surface; split it, and Jersey is the dairy cow breed while New is just N.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey cows are a dairy breed, so milk is what a Jersey produces.

clue.text: Flag-waving grand opening engaging six university cops

indicators.note: holding inside, as gears engage

parts.note: a chasm is a vast opening in the ground

indicators.note: catches, so it takes the other in

explanation.surface: A patriot opens the grand parade as six campus police look on.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times first printed CHAUVINIST here, but the wordplay only builds the -ISM form, which was later marked correct. 'Cops' is the verb, to catch, and 'Flag-waving' works as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A near-synonym by image: waving the national flag stands for the aggressive patriotism named after the legendary French jingoist Nicolas Chauvin.

clue.text: Effective old treasure coffers bolted

indicators.note: used as a verb: locks away inside, as in a coffer

parts.note: a pet = a treasure, a darling

explanation.surface: Old treasure chests were well fastened shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coffers' and 'bolted' paint locked strongboxes; 'coffers' is really a verb and 'bolted' means ran away.
explanation.definitionFit: Operant means operating, having an effect.

clue.text: Killer in plot to pick up woman next door

indicators.note: catch by ear, as you pick up what someone says

explanation.surface: A murderer in a thriller plans to seduce the neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killer in plot' suggests a murder mystery, but the plot is a garden bed and the killer destroys weeds.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbicide kills plants in a garden plot.

clue.text: Play the clarinet with fiddle as a diversion

indicators.note: tamper with, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes up the clarinet and the violin as a hobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' is the violin in the surface but the anagram signal here. All fifteen letters of 'Play the clarinet' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Something said parenthetically is an aside, a diversion from the main point.

clue.text: One regularly spending years in struggle

definitions.text: One regularly spending years in struggle

indicators.note: using up, so the letter is paid out and gone
the letters fight and end up in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone devotes years, steadily, to a long fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an instruction to take alternate letters; it is simply fodder. The whole clue is also the definition: a guerrilla spends years in an armed struggle.
explanation.definitionFit: A guerrilla is an irregular fighter engaged in a long armed struggle.

clue.text: Alarm having time set by mistake

indicators.note: put aside, so that letter is removed

explanation.surface: An alarm clock went off at the wrong hour because it was set incorrectly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an alarm clock set wrong; 'set by' actually means set aside, dropping the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, and the surface's clock set by mistake is itself an error.

clue.text: Wife's supplanted by female in artfully better clothes

indicators.note: pushed out and replaced by

parts.note: to outwit is to get the better of by cunning

explanation.surface: A wife is replaced by another woman who is craftily better dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artfully better' is a verb, to outwit. W and F are the standard abbreviations for wife and female.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a matching set worn together counts as one outfit.

clue.text: Flying ace heading by into base

indicators.note: debased, so the letters are corrupted into a new order
going in front of what follows

parts.note: A = ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A flying ace steers his plane back to base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying ace' reads as one pilot, but splits into the definition and A. 'Base' is an adjective: low, debased.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the activity: 'flying' as a noun, the business of piloting planes.

clue.text: Break black-stemmed pair of tennis racket heads

indicators.note: has a stem inside, so it holds the next piece

parts.note: a racket is a swindle, a con

indicators.note: to head something is to lead it, so this piece goes in front
a pair is two, taken from the front of the word

explanation.surface: A pair of tennis rackets with black handles break their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all tennis kit, but 'racket' here is a swindle, and 'Break' is to disobey a rule. 'Stemmed' means given a stem, so the black piece runs down the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of breaking a law or rule, not smashing an object.

clue.text: Urban housing that hurts duke's land

indicators.note: holds inside it, as a house holds people

parts.note: what you say when something hurts

explanation.surface: A city is housing a duke whose land it is causing pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urban' is an adjective standing in for a noun, the place itself. 'Land' is the verb, as a plane lands.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft touches down when it lands.

clue.text: Catholic doctor unravels source of infection

indicators.note: used as a verb: tamper with, rearrange
a river's source is where it starts, so the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A Catholic physician traces where an infection came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catholic' with a capital suggests the Church, but lower-case catholic means all-embracing. 'Doctor' is the verb, not the physician.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic in its general sense means universal, all-embracing.

clue.text: One end of support, far up from foot

definitions.text: One end of support, far up from foot

indicators.note: a single letter from an end of the word, here the last

explanation.surface: Describing a leg: its top end sits a long way above the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the leg is the body's support, and the thigh is its end furthest from the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes the leg as the body's support, and its upper end, furthest from the foot, is exactly this part.

clue.text: Refugee perhaps cutting a couple of tons of fabric

indicators.note: cutting out, so those letters are removed

parts.words: cutting a couple of tons of

explanation.surface: A refugee is cutting a huge bale of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: T = ton, so 'a couple of tons' is TT, and TEXTILE has exactly two to lose. 'Perhaps' marks a refugee as one example of an exile.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile is someone living away from their homeland, as a refugee may be.

clue.text: CEO briefly engaged in sex on casting couch

indicators.note: said briefly, the word is cut short to an abbreviation
busy in, as a worker is engaged in a job, so it sits inside
metal casting pours material into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A company boss is caught in a casting-couch sex scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casting couch' reads as one phrase, but 'casting' is the anagram signal and 'couch' is the verb, to phrase. An American company's CEO is often its president.
explanation.definitionFit: To couch an idea in certain words is to express it that way.

clue.text: Festival's framing reproduction piece in Sunflowers tribute

indicators.note: surrounding, as a frame surrounds a picture

parts.note: Tet, the Vietnamese New Year festival
the stamen is the pollen-bearing, male reproductive part of a flower

explanation.surface: An arts festival shows a copy of Van Gogh's Sunflowers as a tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all painting: 'reproduction' and 'piece' suggest a copy of Van Gogh, but they are botany, a flower's reproductive part.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of proof that honours something, as in 'a testament to her skill'.

clue.text: Answer short cry from swimmer guards note in the water

indicators.note: a word falling short does not reach its end, so the last letter goes
keeps inside, as a guard surrounds

parts.note: ti, the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A swimmer lets out a brief shout while a lifeguard watches in the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'swimmer' is a duck, not a person, so its cry is QUACK.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquatic means living or happening in water.

clue.text: Left cutting fork out by remaining ham

indicators.note: cutting into, so it sits inside
next to, so the pieces join

parts.note: to fork out is to pay

explanation.surface: Leftover ham is cut up with a fork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like the meat but is the verb: to act too broadly. 'Left' is L, not leftovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre idiom: a hammy actor exaggerates every line, which is overacting the role.

clue.text: Redacted communique because it's province of Nato telecoms

indicators.note: edited down, so only a piece of the words is left

explanation.surface: A military message was censored because it concerned NATO communications.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works two ways: Quebec is a Canadian province, and it is also the word for Q in the NATO phonetic alphabet, the 'province' or domain of military radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Quebec is a Canadian province and the NATO alphabet's word for Q.

clue.text: Take naked massage after raising garment

indicators.note: the wordplay piece named first comes later in the answer, following the other
lifting up, so in a down clue the letters run upward
stripped of its outer letters

parts.note: TAKE without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone strips for a massage after taking off a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' and 'garment' paint undressing, but 'naked' only strips TAKE to AK. 'Raising' reverses, as a down entry reads upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A burka is a full-body garment worn by some Muslim women.

clue.text: Small black gags could be funny

definitions.note: 'a funny' is a noun, a joke

indicators.note: silences by filling the mouth, so it holds the letter inside

explanation.surface: Short, dark jokes can be amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gags' looks like jokes, pointing at the answer, but it is the verb: JET gags S.
explanation.definitionFit: A jest is a joke, and 'a funny' is slang for one.

clue.text: Edition that is covering return of American head of state

indicators.note: wrapping round what follows
coming back, so the letters run the other way
a head sits at the top, so it is the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A newspaper edition reports an American president coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' reads as a president; here it is just the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from publishing: each numbered release of a magazine is an issue.

clue.text: Earl's against parishioner delivering a pound of pickings

parts.note: a lector is a church member who reads the lessons aloud in services

explanation.surface: An aristocrat quarrels with a churchgoer who has handed him a pound's worth of scraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickings' sounds like leftovers, but it means choices made in elections. 'Against' means next to, so E sits beside LECTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Electoral means relating to elections, the picking of representatives.

clue.text: Reaction of terrified swallow after cutting its wings

indicators.note: placed after, so it comes last

parts.note: a cutting wind is a cold one

indicators.note: the two edges, here first and last letters

parts.note: first and last letters of SWALLOW
to swallow food is to eat

explanation.surface: A frightened swallow reacts after someone clips its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' does double duty: once as a verb, and again, through 'its wings', as the bird. 'Cutting' is not a deletion signal; it describes a biting wind.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: fear makes the skin clammy while chilled, so 'break out in a cold sweat' names the terrified body's response.

clue.text: Avid Conservative opposed to Labour changing sides

indicators.note: left swaps to right, so L becomes R

explanation.surface: A keen Tory, opposed to the Labour Party, defects to the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is British party politics: Conservative and Labour are the two main parties. Here 'Labour' is plain work, and the 'sides' are left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy about something is avid for it, as in 'crazy about football'.
